content.text: A computation is a sequence of state transformations carried out according to an effective, finite description of rules. Separating the program, the state, and the environment clarifies what an algorithm actually promises. A finite machine may possess unbounded mathematical storage in its model, while any physical computer has finite memory, finite energy, and a failure-prone clock. The input specification determines what is represented: bit strings, integers, rational numbers, measured reals, or structured graphs. The output specification determines what counts as a result, including error, refusal, and nontermination. A program executable on a laptop is not thereby a proof of the function it computes; its semantics, preconditions, and adversarial cases must be examined. The same observed output may arise from different internal programs. A constructive representation requires state, instruction syntax, transition rules, and a stopping condition. The Computation Atlas treats all those elements as evidence fields, not optional implementation details.

content.text: The Church–Turing thesis relates an informal idea—an effective procedure—to formal mathematical computability. Several formal systems, including Turing machines and lambda calculus, identify the same class of computable functions. Their equivalence is a mathematical result; the interpretation of every intuitively effective process is a thesis rather than an ordinary theorem about a previously formalized concept. This thesis is not the claim that every physical event can be efficiently simulated on today's computers, nor that all imaginable physical processes obey a particular digital implementation. Conflating computability with speed, parallelism, or physical determinism produces misleading forecasts. A human reconstructing the field needs three separate questions: can a function be computed in principle; what resources does it require; and can a particular physical system realize it?

content.text: The halting problem asks for an algorithm that correctly determines for every program and input whether execution eventually stops. A diagonal proof shows no such total algorithm exists under a universal computation model. This is not a warning that no practical termination checker can ever help. What fails is a universal complete decision procedure for arbitrary programs. This distinction guides how to describe software test outcomes and AI agent recovery: “not shown to terminate”, “terminated under bound B”, “proved terminating for a restricted model”, and “observed not to finish” are different evidence states.

Model checking is distinct from running a real distributed system: clock timing, nondeterministic environment input, network loss, and memory corruption may be absent from the abstraction. A preservation-grade report must identify the model boundary and whether the search was complete.

content.text: An invariant is a property of system states preserved by every allowed transition. An inductive invariant requires initialization and step preservation. It is a sufficient proof principle: if the invariant holds initially and no transition leaves it, every reachable state satisfies it. A proposed invariant may fail induction because it is too weak even when the target safety property is true; strengthening is often needed. In an explicitly finite universe, a checker can enumerate transitions and validate an invariant. If a successor leaves the declared universe, rejecting the model is more honest than silently ignoring the transition. The specific set of transitions must be preserved for later auditors to reproduce the proof.

content.text: A ranking function maps nonterminal states to a well-founded set and decreases on every transition. A natural-number rank that strictly decreases cannot decrease forever, proving termination when each transition follows the model and no stuck nonterminal state is allowed. A ranking proof is stronger than observing that many runs stop, but it is conditional on complete state and transition descriptions. Real applications may use lexicographic ranks, multisets, ordinals, or fairness assumptions. An agent's “determination” or intent cannot replace these progress conditions. content.text: Information theory quantifies expected surprise under a declared probability distribution. Shannon entropy H measures average self-information in bits when the logarithm base is two. It does not measure truth, intelligence, understanding, meaning, or scientific evidence quality. A perfectly random source can have high entropy while carrying no useful explanatory content; a compact theorem can have few bytes while conveying profound knowledge to someone with the prerequisites. For compression, probability assumptions and code constraints matter. Empirical frequency estimates introduce sampling uncertainty that should not be hidden inside an exact-looking entropy number. A physical thermodynamic entropy is related in some settings but not interchangeable with Shannon entropy without a specific model.

content.text: A prefix-free binary code has no codeword that begins another codeword. Such a code can be decoded greedily without explicit separators when the codebook is known. This does not by itself ensure efficient compression; code lengths should reflect symbol probabilities, and metadata overhead matters. Huffman coding produces an optimal binary prefix code for a specified finite symbol distribution under ordinary codeword-length cost, but not necessarily an optimal code under streaming, edit resilience, or CPU constraints. Archive survival depends on storing the codebook, version, bit ordering, and integrity metadata. A file that cannot be decoded without a vanished proprietary codec is not meaningfully preserved.

applicability: Algorithms, computer science, software reasoning within declared mathematical model

limitations: No benchmark speedup claim follows from the model alone. Amdahl is also not a universal law of all optimization: workload scaling and changed algorithms alter the question.
content.text: Parallel computing divides work among processors, but dependencies and coordination limit speedup. Amdahl's law models fixed-size work: a fraction remains serial, and the rest can be parallelized ideally. Parallel overhead, data transfer, contention, load imbalance, and memory capacity often make real speedup smaller. Gustafson-style scaling considers larger problems as resources grow, answering a different question. Amdahl's law is not evidence that a particular distributed agent swarm will run proportionally faster. Tasks may share bottlenecks, retry failed work, contend for a provider, or duplicate efforts. Measuring total compute, wall-clock critical path, and quality separately is essential.

Wilson score intervals often behave better than naïve normal intervals near zero or one successes, but neither removes sampling bias, dependence between tasks, evaluator leakage, or measurement error. Paired experimental designs control task difficulty when comparing two agents or algorithms; independent Bernoulli proportions are inappropriate if the same tasks are used with correlated outcomes. content.text: An algorithm should be evaluated against its stated contract, not a convenient benchmark alone. Unit tests check examples and boundary cases; property-based tests examine invariants on many generated inputs; independent oracles use a mathematically or implementationally separate route; differential tests compare systems; formal proofs establish quantified results under assumptions. These forms of evidence have different strengths. Randomized trial counts do not automatically measure independence: two algorithms could share the same bug, and a large number of correlated trials can exaggerate certainty. A benchmark specification should include input generator, distribution, seeds, environment, hardware, compiler versions, numerical tolerances, and expected outputs before results are observed.
